description: The Rise of the Ancient Kemets comes forth the beyond the Galaxy
summary:
PEAKLIGHT is a web tool that compares two lunar landing sites over the same 30-day window and answers one question quickly: when does each site have sunlight, a view of Earth, or both?
The problem: lunar south-polar lighting and Earth visibility change sharply with small shifts in site or date. Existing tools (Quickmap, Moon Trek, JPL Horizons) are powerful but built for specialists.
What it does: one mission clock drives a 3D Moon with the day-night terminator, a horizon panorama per site showing the Sun and Earth (with correct Earth phase), and a shared 30-day timeline of sunlight, Earth visibility and their overlap. A decision table compares sunlit %, Earth in view %, longest darkness, longest Earth outage and peak Sun elevation. An arrival-delay control recomputes both sites to show how a schedule slip changes the result. Optional sound cues mark sunrise, sunset, Earthrise and Earthset.
How it works: an on-device, low-precision lunar and solar ephemeris with libration, sampled every 15 minutes. It runs entirely in the browser.
Limitations: the ephemeris is approximate and not yet validated against JPL Horizons; terrain is a user-set flat horizon mask, not LOLA data; site coordinates are approximate; the 3D surface is illustrative. Results show geometry, not power or link budget.
Next: validate against JPL Horizons, add LOLA horizon masks, and shareable scenario links.
details:
PEAKLIGHT is an interactive web-based tool designed to help users compare potential lunar landing sites based on two important mission factors: solar illumination and Earth visibility.
The tool allows users to select two locations on the Moon or enter custom coordinates, then examine how sunlight and Earth visibility change over a shared 30-day mission window. It calculates the percentage of time each site receives sunlight, the percentage of time Earth remains geometrically visible, and the periods when both conditions are available. Users can also explore the mission timeline, simulate different arrival delays, adjust the assumed terrain horizon, and compare the results through interactive visualizations.
PEAKLIGHT provides a side-by-side comparison supported by a 3D lunar view, a shared timeline, detailed measurements, and data export options in CSV and JSON formats. This can help users understand the advantages and trade-offs of different landing locations during early mission planning.
The project was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Three.js for the interactive 3D visualization. It uses browser-based calculations and is hosted on GitHub Pages.
During development, we explored NASA-recommended resources, including LROC QuickMap, NASA Moon Trek, and NASA JPL Horizons, as well as the Canadian Space Agency's Moon Exploration resources. These platforms provide valuable information about lunar terrain, surface features, and astronomical data. In the current version, however, PEAKLIGHT uses manually entered site coordinates and its own approximate browser-based calculations rather than directly integrating datasets from these platforms.
What makes PEAKLIGHT creative is the combination of solar illumination and Earth visibility in one time-based comparison tool. Instead of evaluating a landing site using only one measurement, it allows users to explore how multiple mission conditions change over time and how arrival delays may affect them.
During development, our team considered mission timing, location coordinates, solar and Earth geometry, assumed terrain horizons, sampling intervals, and the limitations of simplified models. The current calculations are approximate and have not yet been validated against JPL Horizons or real lunar elevation datasets. Therefore, PEAKLIGHT is intended as an educational and preliminary site-comparison tool, not a replacement for professional landing-site analysis.
